summary: The Marine Aquaculture Research for America Act of 2026 (MARA Act of 2026) directs the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to establish an Office of Aquaculture and an assessment program for commercial-scale offshore aquaculture demonstration projects. The bill outlines criteria for issuing, renewing, modifying, or terminating permits for offshore aquaculture facilities in federal waters (the exclusive economic zone), creates a unified federal permitting and review process, provides general support and technical assistance for the aquaculture industry, and mandates specific scientific studies and reports from the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine and the Government Accountability Office.

affected_groups.effect: May experience changes in fishing access and opportunities, and can benefit from priority consideration for permits if negatively impacted by disasters or pandemics.
affected_groups.group: Commercial and recreational fishermen, fishing communities, and seafood workers

affected_groups.effect: Subject to new permitting, reporting, and operational standards while gaining access to grants, technical assistance, regional networks, and commercial-scale demonstration opportunities.
Given opportunities to participate in reviews, enter agreements for similar state waters, request permit modifications, and provide local and traditional knowledge.
affected_groups.group: Coastal States, Indian Tribes, and Native Hawaiian organizations

affected_groups.effect: Required to coordinate, streamline, and participate in a unified rulemaking and review process for offshore aquaculture permits.
affected_groups.group: Federal agencies (NOAA, U.S. Coast Guard, EPA, Army Corps of Engineers, FDA, Departments of Agriculture and the Interior

key_provisions: Establishes an Office of Aquaculture within the National Marine Fisheries Service, including regional representation and dedicated budget requests.
Requires NOAA to establish an assessment program for commercial-scale offshore aquaculture through demonstration projects within 180 days of enactment.
Sets eligibility criteria, application processes, public comment periods, priority considerations, and 10-year permit terms (with renewal options) for offshore aquaculture demonstration projects.
Directs the creation of a unified permitting and review process across multiple federal agencies, designating NOAA as the lead agency.
Imposes mandatory annual reporting requirements for demonstration project participants regarding production, environmental impacts, and safety.
Provides general support for the industry through marketing grants, regional networks, an aquaculture database, and technical assistance programs.
Mandates a study by the Ocean Studies Board of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine and a report by the Government Accountability Office within five years.
missing_information: Specific funding authorization amounts or appropriations levels required to carry out the act.
Exact geographic locations or specific bodies of water where demonstration projects will be sited.
summary_detail.plain_summary: The Marine Aquaculture Research for America Act of 2026 (MARA Act of 2026) directs the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to establish an Office of Aquaculture and an assessment program for commercial-scale offshore aquaculture demonstration projects. The bill outlines criteria for issuing, renewing, modifying, or terminating permits for offshore aquaculture facilities in federal waters (the exclusive economic zone), creates a unified federal permitting and review process, provides general support and technical assistance for the aquaculture industry, and mandates specific scientific studies and reports from the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine and the Government Accountability Office.
summary_detail.significance: The legislation establishes the first comprehensive federal regulatory and assessment framework dedicated specifically to commercial-scale offshore aquaculture in the U.S. exclusive economic zone, impacting federal agency operations, commercial fishing access, and the domestic seafood economy.
